strengths: Well-motivated and clearly identified problem: existing MoE offloading systems assume distinct CPU/GPU memory pools and pipelined/batched execution, both of which are mismatched to UMA-based edge SoCs and batch-size-1 interactive inference; this gap is convincingly demonstrated via latency breakdowns on server vs. edge hardware (Fig. 1).

Novel use of semantically lossless compression (bit-field decomposition of BF16 into low-entropy exponent bits and high-entropy sign-mantissa bits) for MoE expert offloading, motivated by solid empirical entropy/compression analysis (Figs. 2-4), avoiding the behavioral/security risks of quantization that the paper carefully surveys.

Non-trivial theoretical contributions: a constant-factor (3-1/L) approximation guarantee for the proposed cache-affinity DAG scheduling algorithm, and a proof that the rank-based cache-hit probability model derived via iterative proportional fitting achieves maximum entropy (Bayes-robust) consistency with observed marginals.

Comprehensive system implementation (2.6K Python + 8K C++/CUDA) including a hierarchical, compression-state-aware cache manager, DAG-based asynchronous scheduler, and a memory-coalesced GPU tensor-recovery kernel exploiting zero-copy UMA access.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse MoE architectures (decoder-only and encoder-decoder), two edge hardware configurations, multiple batch sizes, and multiple metrics (TPOT, TTFT, throughput, end-to-end latency), showing consistent and often large improvements over representative offloading baselines (Accelerate, DeepSpeed, MoE-Infinity), plus an ablation isolating the cache-planning/eviction design choices.
weaknesses: Baseline selection is questionable: comparisons are limited to general-purpose offloading frameworks (Accelerate, DeepSpeed, MoE-Infinity) rather than the more directly relevant on-device/CPU-GPU hybrid MoE systems explicitly cited in the related work (e.g., Fiddler, KTransformers, SwapMoE, ProMoE, Klotski), making it hard to judge whether the reported gains (up to 6.76x) reflect genuine advances over the true state of the art for edge MoE serving.

The paper does not decompose how much of the speedup stems from lossless compression itself versus the cache-affinity scheduling/hierarchical caching versus implementation-level optimizations (zero-copy, page-cache alignment), so the specific contribution of the compression pipeline is not clearly isolated beyond the caching-only ablation in Fig. 10.

Given the compression ratios achieved are modest (68-74%), the very large end-to-end speedups (up to 42x in some end-to-end latency comparisons) raise questions about whether baselines are weak/poorly configured for edge NVMe offloading rather than ZipMoE being fundamentally superior; more analysis or stronger baselines would strengthen the claims.

No experiment directly verifies bit-exact/semantic losslessness of the system's output relative to the uncompressed model (e.g., confirming identical generations or exact logits), despite the paper's central claim and marketing around avoiding the security/behavioral risks of quantization documented in the introduction.

Evaluation hardware is limited to two Jetson AGX Orin configurations; despite the paper's motivation citing mobile phones, Raspberry Pi, and Apple Silicon as target UMA platforms, no experiments validate generalization to these more resource-constrained or heterogeneous edge devices.

The theoretical scheduling guarantee relies on idealized, uniform per-chunk I/O and decompression cost assumptions (u, c treated as constants); real hardware exhibits variable NVMe latency, page-cache effects, and contention that could weaken the practical tightness of the bound.
The offline compression/initialization cost (time and storage overhead of bit-field decomposition and compression) is not reported, which is relevant for practical deployability and reproducibility.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not engage with the paper's own extensively discussed security motivation (quantization-induced vulnerabilities), a missed opportunity given the paper's stated goal of preserving model behavior for security reasons.
No mention of code/artifact release, and the system involves substantial custom C++/CUDA engineering, which may hinder independent reproducibility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper carefully characterizes the mismatch between existing offloading-based MoE serving systems (designed for server/cloud with distinct CPU/GPU memory) and UMA-based edge SoCs, backed by concrete profiling data (Fig. 1-4) that isolates I/O stalls, decompression-vs-I/O latency, and CPU underutilization.

Technically sound and non-trivial system design: bit-field decomposition into low-entropy exponent bits and high-entropy sign-mantissa bits, a hierarchical compression-state cache (F/C/S/E pools), and a cache-affinity DAG scheduler that overlaps I/O and CPU decompression are all well-motivated by the preliminary measurements.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: a provable (3-1/L)-approximation guarantee for the cache-affinity scheduler (Theorem 3.1, proven in Appendix B) and a maximum-entropy justification for the rank-based cache planning DP (Theorem 3.2, proven in Appendix D) go beyond typical systems papers and lend credibility to the design choices.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three representative MoE architectures (decoder-only and encoder-decoder), two edge hardware configurations, multiple metrics (TTFT, TPOT, throughput, end-to-end latency across output lengths), and strong reported gains (up to 72.77% latency reduction, 6.76x throughput) against multiple established baselines (Accelerate, DeepSpeed, MoE-Infinity) plus an additional recent baseline (FineMoE) in the appendix.

Careful ablations and diagnostic experiments that decompose the sources of improvement (cache heterogeneity vs. cache planning vs. OS page cache contribution), a sensitivity analysis to workload distribution shift, and a comparison across compressor backends, which substantially strengthen the empirical claims and transparency about what drives the gains.

The approach is genuinely lossless (behavior-preserving), addressing a legitimate concern (raised with citations) that lossy quantization can alter model behavior/security properties—this differentiates the contribution from the dominant compression literature.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison in the main text (Accelerate, DeepSpeed, MoE-Infinity) does not include several more specialized on-device/edge MoE serving systems explicitly discussed in the introduction (e.g., Fiddler, Klotski, ProMoE, EdgeMoE, D2MoE, KTransformers); only one additional recent system (FineMoE) is compared, and only in the appendix, limiting confidence that ZipMoE dominates the current state of the art in edge MoE serving broadly.

Hardware generalizability claims (Section 6) are largely speculative — all experiments are run on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (64GB/32GB) variants; no results are shown on other UMA platforms mentioned as motivating targets (Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi, mobile phones), so the claimed broad applicability to 'mobile and edge computing platforms' is not empirically substantiated.

The compression ratio achieved (roughly 66-74% of original size) is relatively modest, and the paper's own ablation (Table 1) shows that the 'core system' (compression + scheduling) contributes ~76% of throughput gains while cache planning contributes ~24%; it would help to further disentangle how much of the reported speedup is attributable to lossless compression per se versus generic systems engineering (zero-copy, better GPU memory management, improved OS page-cache utilization), since Section 5.1 acknowledges several of these compounding factors that are not orthogonal to the core algorithmic contribution.

The rank-based cache planning model assumes expert activation follows Bernoulli trials consistent with a stable marginal rank distribution; while a sensitivity analysis is provided (Appendix E.2), it only tests synthetic smoothing perturbations of the same trace rather than genuinely distributional shifts across different domains/tasks, leaving open how robust the approach is to workloads with different structure (e.g., code vs. chat vs. multi-turn).

No repository link is provided despite claiming 'code is available at:' (left blank), which is a reproducibility concern for a systems paper with substantial implementation complexity (8K lines of C++/CUDA, 2.6K lines of Python).

The theoretical approximation bound (3-1/L) is a worst-case guarantee whose tightness/practical relevance is not empirically validated (e.g., no comparison of achieved ALG/OPT ratio in practice), so it is unclear how informative this bound is for real deployment scenarios beyond providing qualitative assurance.
